claims.text: Controlled alloying can shift the d-band center of a transition-metal catalyst.
Changing the d-band center directly tunes the adsorption energies of key reactants and intermediates.
Adsorption-energy changes caused by d-band-center modification govern catalytic activity and selectivity.
A secondary alloying element can shift the d-band center without drastically changing catalyst morphology.
The alloying-induced electronic modification can be represented by a measurable shift in the d-band-center position.
Spectroscopic techniques can confirm the proposed shift in the d-band center.
An upward shift of the d-band center typically strengthens adsorbate binding.
Stronger adsorbate binding from an upward d-band-center shift may increase activity but can cause overbinding and change selectivity.
A downward shift of the d-band center can weaken adsorbate interactions.
Weaker adsorbate interactions from a downward d-band-center shift may lower activity and alter product distribution.
Relative to the pure-metal baseline, a moderately upshifted d-band center will enhance catalytic activity.
Relative to the pure-metal baseline, a moderately upshifted d-band center will alter selectivity because key intermediates bind more strongly.
Systematic tuning of the d-band center should produce predictable trends in turnover frequency and product ratios.
The proposed relationship applies primarily when the rate-limiting step is controlled by surface adsorbate binding energies.
Significant morphology changes, surface restructuring, or segregation can invalidate or confound the proposed d-band-center relationship.
XPS or UPS measurements can quantify the relevant d-band-center shifts in the proposed alloy series.
A lack of consistent correlation between controlled d-band-center shifts and adsorption energies, activity, or selectivity would falsify the hypothesis.
